1226.title: Sparks from one fire
1226.hook: as sparks fly from one fire and fall back into it, so beings come from the One (Akal Ustat 87)
1226.howItsDone: Sikhs sing this stanza of Akal Ustat in kirtan, and its images of sparks, dust and waves are used in katha to explain how all beings come from and return to the One.

segments.voice: Yesterday, same light in all: temple and mosque, the dress of different lands, and the same eyes underneath. Your line was all the same light.

Late at night at a bonfire, somebody drops another log on, and the fire answers. A column of sparks goes up into the dark. For a second each one is its own bright thing, drifting its own way, a little separate from the rest. Then they fade and fall, and the ones that land in the coals simply become fire again. Kids watch this for a long time without being told to. The stanza right after yesterday's watches it too.
screen: `A LOG ON THE BONFIRE.` → `EACH SPARK ITS OWN WAY.` → `BACK INTO THE COALS.`

segments.voice: Akal Ustat, the next stanza, in paraphrase. As from one fire countless sparks rise up, and, each apart for a while, fall back into the fire. As from one heap of dust the particles fill the air, and settle back into the dust. As from one river countless waves rise, and the waves, being water, are all called water. So from the One, the form of all the world, beings appear; they arise from it, and into it they all merge again. Three pictures, one teaching. The spark says: for a while you really are separate. Bright, moving, your own path through the dark. The stanza doesn't pretend that away. The dust says: even the small, plain, unglamorous bits come from the same heap. Not only the bright ones. And the wave says the boldest thing: even while it's rising, a wave never stops being water. You don't have to wait for the end to belong to the One. You're made of it now. One way Sikhs read it: this is the shape of a life. You come from the One, you live as a spark for a while, and you return. A few days ago, the ninth Guru's hymn ended with a person blending with the Lord like water into water. Here his son sings something close, in images of his own. It finishes the thought of the last two days, too. One human race, the same light: here's why. Everyone you meet is a spark off the same fire.
screen: `SPARKS RISE AND FALL BACK.` · `DUST FROM ONE HEAP.` · `A WAVE IS STILL WATER.` · `FROM THE ONE, BACK TO THE ONE.` · then, large: `SPARKS OF ONE FIRE.`

segments.voice: If it's safe, light a candle or open a video of a fire; if not, close your eyes and remember one. Watch how the flame moves and never quite holds a shape, and let yourself be one spark from it, bright for a while, from the same fire. If you pray, rest in Waheguru on each breath out, and put out any real flame when you're done.
Sparks from one fire. Like sparks from a fire, dust from a heap, waves from a river, beings come from the One and merge in it again. Today's word.
Your line: sparks of one fire. A wave never stops being water. Until tomorrow.

1227.title: Bachitar Natak
1227.hook: his autobiographical poem, the wondrous drama
1227.howItsDone: Sikhs read Bachitar Natak as Guru Gobind Singh's own account of his calling and his early life, and passages from it are told in katha on gurpurabs and at historical gurdwaras.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sparks from one fire: beings rise from the One like sparks, and fall back into it. Your line was sparks of one fire.

Celebrity memoirs tend to open the same way. A childhood street. A first big break. A photo section in the middle. Readers come for the person: me, my story, my wins. Now a different kind of life story. Its author was a Guru, a poet and a leader of armies. He had plenty of wins to tell. And he chose to call his own story a drama, a wondrous one, and to open it somewhere else entirely.
screen: `ME, MY STORY, MY WINS.` → `A GURU WRITES HIS LIFE.` → `HE CALLS IT A DRAMA.`

segments.voice: Bachitar Natak: the wondrous drama. It's a long poem in the Dasam Granth, and in it Guru Gobind Singh tells parts of his own story in his own voice. Here, the tenth Guru says I. But look where it begins. Not with a birth, not with a battle. It opens with praise. It bows, in paraphrase, to the holy sword, and to the Timeless One whom the poet sees in the sword's strength, the One who cuts down wrong and protects the good. The praise goes on at length before the poet says much about himself at all. Then the story widens before it narrows. He tells of an ancient lineage, the old families that, tradition says, the Gurus' line came from. He tells of a life before this life: a time of deep meditation in the mountains, absorbed in the One, until he was called and sent into the world, to stand up for dharma, for what is right. Only then does he arrive at his birth. Why a drama? A drama is a play with a director. The actors are real, the danger is real, the costumes are real, but someone else wrote the play. The Guru tells his life as a scene inside God's larger play. The wonder isn't him. The wonder is the play he found himself sent into. That frames what this block reads in Bachitar Natak next: what he says about himself, a battle he fought, and his father. All of it told by someone who begins with praise and sees himself as a part in the play.
screen: `THE TENTH GURU SAYS I.` · `IT OPENS WITH PRAISE.` · `A LIFE BEFORE, AND A CALLING.` · `A SCENE IN GOD'S PLAY.` · then, large: `THE WONDROUS DRAMA.`

segments.voice: If you told your life in one page, what would the first line be? Let the usual answers come, where you were born, what you've done, then try opening with what holds you: thanks, wonder, the people who carried you before you could walk. If you pray, rest in Waheguru.

1228.title: Don't call me God
1228.hook: he says whoever calls him God will fall; he is only the servant of the Supreme (Bachitar Natak 6)
1228.howItsDone: Sikhs quote these lines from Bachitar Natak to show that the Gurus are revered as messengers of the divine word while God alone is worshiped.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bachitar Natak, the Guru's life told as one scene in God's play. Your line was the wondrous drama.

Fans can get carried away. A singer, a coach, a preacher, a founder: first they're admired, then adored, and before long people are saying things about them that no human being should hear. Some leaders enjoy it. Some quietly let it grow. In Bachitar Natak, the tenth Guru sees this coming. He has just told how he was sent into the world. And right there, before anyone can get carried away, he draws a hard line.
screen: `ADMIRED, THEN ADORED.` → `SOME LET IT GROW.` → `HE DRAWS A HARD LINE.`

segments.voice: Here are the lines, in paraphrase. Whoever calls me the Supreme Lord will fall into the pit of hell. Know me as His servant, and have no doubt about it. I am the servant of the Supreme Being, and I have come to see the play of the world. Three things stand out. First, the warning isn't soft. He doesn't say, please don't. He says the one who calls him God will fall. The danger he names isn't to his reputation; it's to the person who makes the mistake. Second, the word he chooses for himself: das, servant. Not a modest title for a great man, but the plain word for someone who serves. The Guru of the Sikhs, the leader of the Khalsa, and his name for himself in his own life story is the servant of the Supreme. Third, it fits yesterday. He came, he says, to see the play of the world: tamasha, a spectacle, a show. The servant is in the play. He's not the playwright. Sikhs hold the Guru in deep reverence, and they also hold this line close. The Gurus are honored as the ones who carry God's word, and God alone is worshiped. Guru Gobind Singh writes that boundary into his own story so nobody can blur it later. In the same passage, he adds that he speaks what the Lord tells him to speak, and he does not keep quiet out of fear of anyone. Humble about who he is, bold about what he's been given to say, both at once. That's the servant.
screen: `WHOEVER CALLS ME GOD WILL FALL.` · `DAS: THE SERVANT.` · `IN THE PLAY, NOT ITS AUTHOR.` · `HUMBLE ABOUT HIMSELF, BOLD IN HIS WORD.` · then, large: `ONLY THE SERVANT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you've done that you're proud of, a meal, a kid you helped raise, a hard thing you finished, and let the pride be there. Then trace what made it possible, the teachers, the hands before yours, the breath you didn't make, and let some of the credit travel to them and, if this is your way, to the One. If you pray, rest in Waheguru on each breath out.

1229.title: Bhangani in his words
1229.hook: he describes the battle of Bhangani in vivid verse (Bachitar Natak 8)
1229.tomorrow: He gave his head, not his faith
1229.howItsDone: Sikhs read the account of Bhangani in Bachitar Natak as the tenth Guru's own record of a battle he did not seek, and its names are remembered in katha and Sikh histories.

segments.voice: Yesterday, don't call me God: the tenth Guru names himself the servant, come to see the play of the world. Your line was only the servant.

War stories usually reach us secondhand. A historian's summary, a movie, an uncle who heard it from someone. Rarely does the person at the center pick up a pen and tell it, beat by beat, in verse. In Bachitar Natak, Guru Gobind Singh does that for a battle fought at a place called Bhangani. He names the men who stood with him. He writes the noise. He doesn't hide that arrows came at him too.
screen: `WAR STORIES, SECONDHAND.` → `THE GURU PICKS UP THE PEN.` → `A BATTLE AT BHANGANI.`

segments.voice: Here is the outline of his account, in paraphrase. Fateh Shah, a hill king, comes against him, and the Guru writes that he came without cause. The two sides meet. And then the verse changes speed. The meters quicken, the lines clatter like hooves, and the poem names people. His kinsman Sango Shah fights hard and falls. His uncle Kirpal goes into the fight with a heavy club, and the Guru describes him like a warrior from the old epics. A chief on the other side, Hari Chand, looses arrows, and the Guru writes that one reached him, and that he answered with arrows of his own. In the end the hill forces break, and the Guru gives the victory to the grace of the Timeless One. Why is this in a book Sikhs hold sacred? Three things. First, honesty. He doesn't paint himself as untouchable. He was hit. Kinsmen died. The cost is in the poem. Second, honor for others. Kinsmen and companions are named, so they're remembered. Third, the frame from two days ago. This is a scene in the wondrous drama, and its hero isn't him. He came through, he says, because the One carried him through. Sikh tradition remembers Bhangani as a battle the Guru didn't seek and fought to defend his people. You don't have to love battle poetry to take something from it. A hard day, told truthfully, names the cost, names who stood with you, and gives thanks for getting to the other side.
screen: `A HILL KING COMES WITHOUT CAUSE.` · `THE VERSE QUICKENS; MEN ARE NAMED.` · `HE WAS HIT; HE ANSWERED.` · `THE COST, THE COMPANIONS, THE GRACE.` · then, large: `THROUGH THE BATTLE.`

segments.voice: Choose one day that was a battle in its own way, a diagnosis, a layoff, a long night in a waiting room, and tell it to yourself the way the Guru tells Bhangani: what it cost, and who stood with you, by name. Then notice that you're here, on the other side of it. If you pray, rest in Waheguru with thanks on each breath out.
Bhangani in his words. The tenth Guru's own verse account of a battle: honest about the cost, generous to those beside him, grateful to the One who carried him through. Today's word.

1230.title: He gave his head, not his faith
1230.hook: of his father he writes that he gave his head but not his faith (Bachitar Natak 5)
1230.howItsDone: Sikhs recall these lines from Bachitar Natak when they remember the martyrdom of Guru Tegh Bahadur, and sis dia par sirar na dia is quoted in katha and kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhangani in his words: the cost, the companions, and the grace that carried him through. Your line was through the battle.

At a funeral, the hardest speech belongs to the child. Everyone is waiting to hear what the son or daughter will say: which memory, which word, which part of the life to hold up. Guru Gobind Singh lost his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, to an execution in Delhi. When he came to tell his own life in verse, in Bachitar Natak, he gave his father a few lines. They are short, and every word is chosen.
screen: `THE CHILD'S EULOGY.` → `A SON WHOSE FATHER WAS EXECUTED.` → `A FEW LINES, EVERY WORD CHOSEN.`

segments.voice: Here are the lines, in paraphrase. He protected their forehead mark and their sacred thread, and did a great deed in this dark age. For the sake of the holy, he gave his head, and did not cry out. For the sake of dharma, he did this deed: he gave his head, but not his faith. Look at who the first line protects. Those were the signs of another community's worship, not his own. The son remembers his father dying for someone else's right to pray. Then the pair at the center: he gave his head, sis dia, but not his sirar. Sirar is a word Sikhs gloss as his faith, his resolve, the inner thing that can't be handed over. The body could be taken. That couldn't. The Guru goes on: he writes that his father would not do tricks to save himself. The people of God, he says in paraphrase, are ashamed to perform a juggler's wonders. No miracle show for an emperor, just a man who wouldn't move. And then an image: he broke the clay pot of his body on the head of the king of Delhi, and went to the Lord's own place. A clay pot, smashed. Some readers hear in it that the death landed on the one who ordered it, and that the father walked on, unbroken, into God's presence. For a son, this is grief turned into witness. He doesn't dwell on the blade; he tells you what his father kept. Days ago, telling the ninth Guru's stand for freedom of conscience, this path borrowed one of these lines in passing. Today the whole passage gets its own hearing, in his son's voice.
screen: `THEIR MARK, THEIR THREAD.` · `HEAD, BUT NOT SIRAR.` · `NO JUGGLER'S WONDERS.` · `THE CLAY POT BROKEN.` · then, large: `HEAD, NOT FAITH.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself, gently: what is one thing in me I wouldn't hand over? Not a possession but a principle: honesty with a child, fairness at work, standing up for someone else's right to be who they are. Let it come into focus and see yourself holding it, no drama, just not moving; if you pray, rest in Waheguru on each breath out.

1231.title: The Zafarnama's opening
1231.hook: the letter to Aurangzeb begins with praise of God in Persian verse (Zafarnama)
1231.howItsDone: The Zafarnama is included in the Dasam Granth; Sikhs read and recite it in its original Persian and in translation, and its opening is read as praise of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a son's lines for his father: he gave his head, but not his faith. Your line was head, not faith.

The draft sits on the screen. It's to someone who wronged you badly, someone with power. The first line you typed is all heat: how could you. Plenty of people have written that first line and deleted it at two in the morning. Guru Gobind Singh wrote a letter like this to the emperor Aurangzeb. He wrote it in Persian, the language of the emperor's court, in verse. And the first thing he put on the page wasn't the emperor at all.
screen: `THE LETTER TO SOMEONE WITH POWER.` → `ALL HEAT IN THE FIRST LINE.` → `THE GURU'S LETTER BEGINS ELSEWHERE.`

segments.voice: The letter is the Zafarnama, which you met on day ninety-two. Tradition says it was carried to the emperor by a Sikh messenger, and that it was written in a season of great loss. Its hard words come tomorrow. Today, only its opening, and the opening is praise. In paraphrase, the first lines call on God as perfect in wonders, eternal and generous, the giver of contentment, the provider, the deliverer, the merciful. The Lord who gives without being asked, who holds the earth and the sky, who keeps the whole world fed. Line after line, the names keep coming before a single word goes to the man the letter is for. Notice the language. Persian, and names for God like the Merciful, the Provider, the Generous: names the emperor's own faith also uses. It's the move Akal Ustat made a few days ago: different names, one Lord. The Guru begins the letter on ground the two men share. And the praise frames everything after it. Before any complaint, the letter sets the scene: there is a Judge above both of us, and you and I stand in front of Him. Whatever comes next, a rebuke, a reminder, a demand for honesty, it comes inside that frame. That's not flattery of God to soften the blow. It sets the whole quarrel under Someone greater than either man. Whatever he'd been through, the Guru's first act on the page was to praise. The anger is real, and it's coming. But it doesn't get the first word.

1232.title: Broken oaths
1232.hook: he reproaches the emperor's officers who swore safe passage and broke it (Zafarnama)
1232.howItsDone: Sikhs read and recite the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh's Persian letter to the emperor Aurangzeb, and its lines on broken oaths are often recalled in katha and in teaching about truthful living and keeping one's word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Zafarnama's opening: a letter to an emperor that starts with God, not with grievance. Your line was begin with praise.

A promise is the cheapest thing in the world to make. It costs a breath. It is also one of the few things that can't be bought back once it's broken. Tradition tells it like this. Anandpur had been under siege for a long time. Food was gone. Word came from the emperor's side: leave the fort, and you will have safe passage. Oaths were sworn, tradition says, on what each side held holy. The Guru's household and his Sikhs went out into the night. And once they were out, the armies fell on them. The praise is finished. In the next stretch of his letter, Guru Gobind Singh turns to the oath.
screen: `A PROMISE COSTS A BREATH.` → `LEAVE, AND YOU'LL BE SAFE.` → `ONCE OUTSIDE, THE ATTACK.`

segments.voice: The Zafarnama is written in Persian verse, and this part of it is plain speaking. Paraphrased, the Guru says: I had no trust in your oath. Your officers swore in God's name, and their words were false. A man who breaks his oath, he writes, cannot be trusted with anything. Notice what he doesn't do. He doesn't curse the emperor's faith. He holds the emperor to it. You call on God, he says, in effect; then keep the promises you make in God's name. The standard he reaches for is one the emperor already claims. That makes the letter harder to wave away, because it isn't an outsider's insult. It's a mirror. Some readers notice that the letter is written after terrible loss, and yet the charge is precise. Not you are evil, but you gave your word and broke it. A grievance that names one clear wrong can be answered. A grievance that names everything usually can't. And for Sikhs the oath runs the other way too. In the Gurus' teaching, truthful living stands above clever speech, and the Khalsa is asked to be someone whose word holds. The Zafarnama's anger at broken oaths is also a picture of the opposite: a person, or a people, who keep theirs. Look back over the week. Sparks from one fire. The wondrous drama. Only the servant. Through the battle at Bhangani. Head, not faith. Begin with praise. Read together, they sketch one person: a servant who praises first, names the cost, and stands behind his words.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one promise you've made that's still open, a call you said you'd return, something you told a child, and hold it without scolding yourself, like a ticket you haven't used yet. If you pray, hold that promise before Waheguru as you breathe out.
